video_title: Why Younger Generations Are Convinced They Are Falling Behind | Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak
gist: BCG global chief economist Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak defends his paper 'The Kids Are All Right', arguing age-aligned, inflation-adjusted data show Gen Z and millennials ahead of prior generations on income and wealth, with homeownership delayed (millennials catch Gen X by 42) rather than denied, and that the 'K-shaped economy' lacks a downward leg. Hosts Demetri Kofinas and Grant Williams push back on hedonics, parental support, family-formation costs and the squeezed middle, and attribute record youth pessimism to social media, inflated expectations ($600k 'success' benchmark) and post-GFC financial nihilism.

themes.theme: Gen Z and millennials are ahead, not behind

insights.claim: On an age-aligned, inflation-adjusted basis, Gen Z and millennials have higher incomes and somewhat stronger balance sheets than Gen X, boomers and the silent generation had at the same age, contradicting the 'failed generation' narrative.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Young-cohort consumer purchasing power is structurally stronger than the narrative implies; don't underwrite consumer theses on generational-decline assumptions.
insights.quote: On the income side, Gen Z and millennials are not doing worse than prior generations. They're actually ahead in terms of income at a given age

insights.claim: The median inflation-adjusted income of the oldest Gen Z workers (around age 28) is about 25% higher than millennials and 50% higher than baby boomers at the same age, per the BCG paper.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Hard datapoint supporting the spending power of the youngest earning cohort, relevant for consumer discretionary exposure.

insights.claim: Young cohorts hold more equity and less real estate than prior generations did at the same age, and that equity tilt has been a 'winning ticket' over the last ~15 years, showing up in their wealth curves.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Young-cohort wealth is unusually equity-beta-sensitive: a major equity drawdown would hit their balance sheets (and sentiment/spending) harder than prior generations'.
insights.quote: Having that greater exposure to the equity asset class is something that has been a winning ticket

insights.claim: Real net worth of young (under-35) households went roughly sideways-to-down for about thirty years from around 1990, then jumped post-pandemic from roughly $16,000 to about $39,000-40,000, which Carlsson-Szlezak attributes mostly to stimulus checks plus forced lower spending during COVID.
insights.speaker: Grant Williams (co-host)
insights.so_what: The post-COVID young wealth jump is largely a one-off stimulus artifact and may partly mean-revert in newer Fed data releases.

insights.claim: Baby boomers enjoyed a one-time structural tailwind from women entering the labor force and creating dual-income households; that shift has topped out, so Gen X had less of it and millennials have none, making 'boomers had it better' partly a non-repeatable comparison.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Household income growth can no longer lean on rising labor-force participation of women; future gains must come from productivity and real wages.
insights.quote: But that's a shift that can only happen once. You can't repeat that.

insights.claim: Generational angst about money is perennial: the BCG paper opens with a quote complaining that 'it requires a little fortune now to buy a house' and that furniture costs three times what it did ten years earlier, which dates from 1866.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Treat youth-affordability doom narratives as a recurring cultural constant rather than a new regime signal.
insights.quote: It's from 1866. It's 160 years old, this quote

insights.claim: Millennials' homeownership rate catches up with Gen X's by around age 42, coinciding with a move from expensive urban cores to suburbs; the delay reflects longer education, career-building and a chosen preference for cities.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Housing demand from millennials is deferred rather than lost, supporting suburban/exurban housing demand as the cohort ages into their 40s.
insights.quote: So millennials' homeownership rate catches up with Gen X at the age of 42.

insights.claim: About 90% of Gen Z and millennials want to live in urban areas or close-in suburbs where housing is most supply-constrained and expensive, so poor early affordability is partly self-selected.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Urban rental demand from young cohorts stays strong; affordability stress is concentrated in supply-constrained metros rather than nationwide.

insights.claim: Holding home size constant, affordability of a same-size home has been roughly flat over the last twenty to thirty years; the perceived collapse in affordability is largely driven by expectations of homes roughly 50-60% larger and higher-spec than a generation ago.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Affordability metrics based on median home prices overstate deterioration; product mix (size/quality) matters for homebuilders and housing policy analysis.

insights.claim: The hosts push back that the constant-size comparison smells like hedonic adjustment, and Carlsson-Szlezak concedes it hits a limit because smaller 1960s-70s-style homes are scarcely available today.
insights.speaker: Grant Williams (co-host) / Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Supply of entry-level small homes is a genuine gap, pointing to an opportunity/need for starter-home construction.
insights.quote: That smells of hedonic adjustments, which are real, by the way. Not sufficient.

insights.claim: Not buying in New York City fifteen years ago was likely a financial blessing: many NYC apartments delivered flat or negative real (even nominal) returns over 10-15 years after leverage, maintenance and carry costs, so renting can build more wealth.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Expensive-metro condo ownership has been a poor investment after carry; homeownership is not automatically a wealth builder.
insights.quote: There are tons of apartments in the New York City market that over ten, fifteen years have negative real returns or worse, negative nominal returns.

insights.claim: Kofinas argues residential real estate is historically lower-volatility and more stabilizing than equities, so younger families' heavier reliance on the stock market may make wealth accumulation more precarious; Carlsson-Szlezak counters that housing also crashed in the GFC with leverage and that neither asset class offers total protection.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Sequence risk in equities is now a key driver of young-household wealth, a point to weigh against housing-leverage risk.

themes.theme: Sentiment-spending divergence and the macro read

insights.claim: University of Michigan and Conference Board consumer confidence surveys are at or near record lows even as real consumption is at record highs, with more than $1 trillion of real consumption added since COVID.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Sentiment surveys have become a poor predictor of actual spending; don't trade consumer weakness off confidence data alone.
insights.quote: these are at record lows even as real consumption is at record highs

insights.claim: Full bars and restaurants reflect real wage gains: since about 2022, as inflation came down, real wage growth has been strong, though real wage gains have stalled over the last ~18 months as nominal wage growth cooled and inflation bounced back.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: The real-wage tailwind behind consumption is fading, a watch item for consumer discretionary in the next leg.

insights.claim: Last earnings season showed strong earnings across virtually all subsectors, not just a few tech firms, which he argues is impossible without broad-based consumption rather than spending by a wealthy few.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Breadth of earnings is evidence against a narrow 'rich-only' consumer; supports broader equity exposure beyond megacap tech.

insights.claim: Consumers stay price-sensitive rather than retrenching: when quick-service restaurants took too much price too fast, traffic slumped and spending shifted elsewhere, but total spending continued.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Pricing power is limited in categories that over-raised prices; expect share shifts rather than aggregate demand collapse.

insights.claim: Despite tariffs, the Iran energy shock and higher interest rates, the US economy did not falter, which he argues shows it was in reasonable shape in January 2025 rather than brittle.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Resilience through multiple shocks argues for skepticism toward recession calls.

insights.claim: The repeatedly 'inevitable' recession, including on The Economist's cover, never arrived; macro doom narratives persist because media amplifies the worst tail of the distribution while the aggregate stays resilient.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Fading consensus doom narratives has been a profitable stance; anecdote-driven bearishness is a recurring false alarm.
insights.quote: Nobody clicks on pieces that are balanced and rational. People click on pieces that are outrageous and sound like a scandal.

insights.claim: Kofinas notes the economy has gone through one and is in the midst of a second hiking cycle without a material hit to spending or consumer behavior, which is beginning to undermine his own thesis that zero rates permanently shifted youth toward present consumption.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Monetary tightening has had weaker-than-expected transmission to consumers, relevant for rate-sensitivity assumptions.

themes.theme: K-shaped economy: only the top arm is real

insights.claim: Indexing incomes and balance sheets of income and wealth quintiles/quartiles to 2020 shows the rich getting richer but the bottom also improving; there is no official data showing the poor getting poorer, so the 'K' lacks its downward leg.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: The bottom of the consumer distribution is not in absolute decline, contradicting a key bearish framing for low-end retail and consumer credit.
insights.quote: The rich are getting richer, the poor are not getting poorer. There is no data to support that.

insights.claim: Real wage growth since around 2015, and especially in the post-GFC tight labor markets since about 2017, has been particularly strong at the bottom of the distribution, where early-career earners sit.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Low-wage worker income growth underpins entry-level consumption; watch whether the labor market loosens.

insights.claim: Roughly a quarter of all wage earners see negative real wage growth in any given year, but that was equally true in 2015 and 2005, so it is not new evidence of deterioration.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Anecdotes of falling wages are a constant base rate, not a regime change signal.
insights.quote: A quarter of all employees in a given year has negative real wage growth, but guess what? That's also true of 2015 and that's also true of 2005.

insights.claim: Kofinas counters (citing Mike Green's work) that the true losers are in the middle of the income distribution: middle earners don't access the public benefits available to the poor while facing family-formation costs, so the K's bottom leg may be the middle class.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Middle-income households may be the most stressed consumer segment, relevant for mid-tier retail and political risk.

insights.claim: BCG's corporate clients focused on the consumer were initially suspicious of the 'no downward K' finding, but three to four years of consistently growing consumption have borne it out.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Corporate consensus was too bearish on the consumer; a contrarian datapoint that has been validated.

themes.theme: Inequality, inheritance and the limits of the data

insights.claim: There is no evidence that inequality within Gen Z or millennials exceeds that of prior generations; if anything it may be lower because the young have mostly not yet received inheritances, a major driver of US wealth inequality.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: The coming intergenerational wealth transfer will widen within-cohort inequality among the young, supporting wealth-management and high-end consumer demand.
insights.quote: Inheriting is a big driver of inequality in the United States.

insights.claim: Parental support (cosigning leases, supplemental income, housing help) is likely significant and probably larger than in the past but isn't systematically captured in data; Carlsson-Szlezak argues it doesn't move the aggregate curves materially.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: A hidden transfer channel inflating young urban lifestyles; a data blind spot when modeling young-consumer income.

insights.claim: The paper's analysis is weakest on family formation: childcare, education and healthcare costs for young families, and baby boomers' easier access to familial childcare, aren't separately analyzed, which the hosts flag as a gap.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Young parents may face a squeeze the aggregate data hides, relevant to childcare, education and housing-size demand.

themes.theme: Expectations, social media and youth pessimism

insights.claim: A 2024 survey found Gen Z believes it takes about $600,000 a year to be financially successful, roughly a top-1% income, versus about $150,000 for boomers, with expectations rising progressively in younger generations.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Inflated aspirational benchmarks fuel dissatisfaction and aspirational/luxury spending among the young.
insights.quote: Gen Z think you need to make $600,000 a year to be financially successful, which is what one in 100 Americans make

insights.claim: Gen Z is the 'guinea pig' generation of smartphones and social media without guardrails; algorithmic exposure to luxury lifestyles has skewed perceptions of success and fuels the expectations gap.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Social-media-driven expectations shape young consumer behavior and political sentiment.

insights.claim: Youth-minus-old pessimism is now at an extreme with the young far more pessimistic than older people for the first time, and the series fell off a cliff in 2016 and 2024-25, both coinciding with Donald Trump's election wins.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Youth sentiment readings are partly partisan/political and should be discounted as an economic signal.

insights.claim: Carlsson-Szlezak is optimistic we may have seen peak social media and smartphone culture, as school smartphone bans and policy shifts mean younger cohorts are growing up with guardrails.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: A possible secular reversal in youth smartphone/social media intensity is a long-run risk to engagement-driven platforms.
insights.quote: quite possibly we've seen peak social media and peak smartphone culture

insights.claim: Inflation is felt as a 'silent thief' while wage gains are credited to personal merit, so people don't mentally offset them; even with wages up more than prices (affordability slightly better at the end of the Biden administration than the start), frustration over prices persists.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Price-level resentment is a durable political force regardless of real-wage math, sustaining populist and affordability-focused policy risk.

insights.claim: Carlsson-Szlezak links the overlap between crypto trading and Gen Z to heavy social media use and get-rich-quick content, and Kofinas suggests crypto widens wealth disparities within young cohorts.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Young-cohort crypto exposure is driven by social/narrative flows, implying sentiment-driven, high-variance outcomes.

insights.claim: Kofinas frames 'financial nihilism' as rooted in millennial contempt for the system after the 2008 crisis, with crypto as 'patient zero' and meme-stock episodes (GameStop, AMC, Tesla) driven as much by a thirst for community as by wealth-seeking.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Community- and narrative-driven flows can detach prices from fundamentals for extended periods.
insights.quote: crypto was patient zero for financial nihilism

insights.claim: Kofinas argues systematic passive flows and central banks' post-GFC responses reinforced a belief that fiat is 'toilet paper', pushing youth toward YOLO bets over savings accounts or DCF-based valuation, though prices eventually reconcile with fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Structural flow and monetary drivers underpin speculative regimes; eventual reconciliation implies downside for narrative assets.

insights.claim: Kofinas distinguishes the current AI capex cycle from financial nihilism: it reflects traditional exuberance about the future rather than an embrace of pure Ponzis.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: AI investment boom should be analyzed as a classic exuberance/overbuild cycle, not a meme-style bubble.

insights.claim: Carlsson-Szlezak is not in the camp that equities are a bubble about to pop: valuations are strong but have come down while earnings are very strong, and over a 10-30 year horizon he would 'unequivocally' bet equities remain a wealth-building vehicle.
insights.speaker: Philipp Carlsson-Szlezak (BCG global chief economist)
insights.so_what: Long-horizon equity bull case from a mainstream macro economist despite near-term correction risk.
insights.quote: I'm not in the camp that this is a bubble about to pop
